topic: Day 2 · Toxins, the Kidney & Recovery — Closing the Loop
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician and nephrologist who closes every teaching block with the same refrain — treat the mechanism, protect the kidney, and never let an AKI survivor walk out without a follow-up plan.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case that closes the conference

A 46-year-old man is brought in at 4am, deeply drowsy, tachypnoeic, smelling faintly of alcohol. He was found beside an empty bottle of car antifreeze. The gas: pH 7.12, HCO₃⁻ 8, anion gap 29, lactate mildly raised. Chemistry: measured osmolality 340, calculated 305 — an osmolar gap of 35. His kidneys are already failing. Over the next hours he will either get an antidote and dialysis and walk out, or go blind and die of a metabolic acidosis nobody joined up. This final session ties the whole 16-session arc together: the toxins that poison the kidney and the acid–base system at once, the drugs we must stop, and the myth that nearly kills more AKI survivors than any single toxin — that 'AKI is fully reversible.' We close the loop from the first sepsis lecture to this last antifreeze bottle.

1 · 🧪 Toxic alcohols — the osmolar-gap-THEN-anion-gap timeline

Methanol (windscreen wash, illicit spirits) and ethylene glycol (antifreeze) are themselves relatively harmless small alcohols. The danger is what the liver makes of them. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts them into toxic acids — and the timing of the poisoning is written in a moving pair of gaps.

The mechanism, drawn out

  • Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid — formic acid is directly toxic to the optic nerve (blindness, "snowfield" vision) and the basal ganglia.
  • Ethylene glycol → glycoaldehyde → glycolic acid → oxalic acid — glycolic acid drives the acidosis; oxalate binds calcium (hypocalcaemia) and precipitates as calcium-oxalate crystals in the renal tubules → AKI. Envelope-shaped crystals in the urine are the clue.
🎯 The two gaps move in sequence — this IS the diagnosis

Early (parent alcohol still intact): a large osmolar gap (the unmetabolised small alcohol) with a NORMAL anion gap — the acids have not been made yet. Late (alcohol metabolised): the osmolar gap closes as the parent alcohol is consumed, and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis opens as formic/glycolic acid accumulates. A patient caught in between has both. So a normal osmolar gap does not exclude late toxic-alcohol poisoning, and a normal anion gap does not exclude early poisoning — you must think about the timeline.

Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap first, anion gap later. Treat on suspicion — do not wait for the anion gap to prove it, because by then the optic nerve or kidney is already damaged.

Treatment — block the enzyme, then remove the poison

  • Fomepizole — the antidote. It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, halting conversion of the parent alcohol to its toxic acid metabolites, buying time. (Ethanol infusion is the older alternative where fomepizole is unavailable — it competes for the same enzyme.) Give it on clinical suspicion + osmolar gap; do not wait for levels.
  • Haemodialysis — removes both the parent alcohol and the toxic acids, and corrects the acidosis. Indicated for significant acidosis, AKI/end-organ toxicity (visual symptoms), or high measured levels.
  • Cofactors — folinic acid (methanol, speeds formate breakdown); thiamine and pyridoxine (ethylene glycol, divert glyoxylate away from oxalate).
⚠️ The osmolar gap is a rule-IN, not a rule-OUT

A normal osmolar gap (<10) is falsely reassuring late in the course, once the alcohol has been metabolised to acid — the gap has closed but the patient is now most acidotic and most damaged. Conversely, the "normal" range is wide, so a real ingestion can start with a gap that looks only mildly raised. Use the osmolar gap to raise suspicion, treat empirically with fomepizole when the story fits, and let the evolving anion gap and the clinical picture — not a single normal osmolar gap — guide you.

2 · 💊 Salicylate toxicity — the mixed disorder that fools everyone

Aspirin overdose is the classic mixed acid–base emergency and a direct callback to session 14. Salicylate does two opposing things at once:

  1. Directly stimulates the medullary respiratory centre → hyperventilation → primary respiratory alkalosis (early, and often the first sign — the tachypnoeic, tinnitus-y patient).
  2. Uncouples oxidative phosphorylation and drives organic acid production → primary high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (lactate + ketones + salicylate itself).

So the classic adult picture is a near-normal or high pH with a low pCO₂ AND a low bicarbonate and a raised anion gap — two primary disorders coexisting. (Children and late/severe adult cases tip into a dominant acidaemia, which is an ominous sign.)

⚠️ Acidaemia in salicylate poisoning is a red flag — protect the pH

The ionised, un-protonated salicylate cannot cross membranes; the protonated form can. As the blood becomes more acidic, more salicylate becomes protonated and crosses into the brain — worsening toxicity and seizures. This is why letting the patient become acidaemic (e.g. by intubating and under-ventilating them, stripping away their protective respiratory alkalosis) can be catastrophic. If you must intubate, match their high minute ventilation meticulously.

Treatment — alkalinise the urine, then dialyse

  • Urinary alkalinisation with IV sodium bicarbonate — raising urine pH to ~7.5–8 keeps salicylate ionised and trapped in the tubule ("ion trapping"), massively increasing renal excretion. Also keeps the blood pH up, keeping salicylate out of the brain. Replace potassium — you cannot alkalinise the urine if the patient is hypokalaemic (the kidney reabsorbs K⁺ in exchange for H⁺, acidifying the urine).
  • Haemodialysis — the definitive treatment for severe toxicity. Salicylate is small, water-soluble and minimally protein-bound at toxic levels — ideally dialysable.
🎯 Haemodialysis thresholds in salicylate poisoning

Dialyse for: level >700 mg/L (~5.1 mmol/L) in acute poisoning (lower if chronic/symptomatic), altered mental status/seizures, pulmonary or cerebral oedema, renal failure, severe acidaemia refractory to bicarbonate, or clinical deterioration despite optimal care. Do not anchor on the number alone — a rising level or neurology trumps a 'sub-threshold' concentration.

3 · 🩺 Dialyzable toxins — the mnemonic that saves a poisoned patient

When a poison is causing organ failure, the question is always: can we dialyse it out? A toxin is dialysable if it is small, water-soluble, minimally protein-bound, and has a small volume of distribution (i.e. it stays in the blood where the dialyser can reach it). The high-yield list:

💡 The dialysable-toxins mnemonic — "I STUMBLED" / classic ISTUMBLE

Isopropanol · Salicylates · Theophylline · Uraemia · Methanol (and the other toxic alcohols/ethylene glycol) · Barbiturates · Lithium · Ethylene glycol. Add the two great metabolic offenders modern toxicology emphasises: metformin (lactic acidosis) and valproate. The workhorse six to actually remember on-call: Lithium, Metformin/lactate, Salicylate, toxic alcohols (methanol/ethylene glycol), Valproate, Theophylline.

ToxinWhy dialyseClue at the bedside
LithiumSmall ion, renally cleared; toxicity in AKI/dehydrationTremor, confusion, seizures; narrow therapeutic index
MetforminRemoves drug AND corrects the lactic acidosis it causesSevere high-lactate HAGMA in AKI (MALA)
SalicylateSmall, water-soluble, low protein binding at toxic levelsMixed resp alkalosis + HAGMA, tinnitus
Toxic alcoholsRemoves parent alcohol + toxic acids; corrects acidosisOsmolar gap then anion gap; visual loss / oxalate crystals
ValproateSaturable protein binding — free fraction rises and becomes dialysable in overdoseComa, hyperammonaemia, high level
TheophyllineSmall, low volume of distributionVomiting, tachyarrhythmia, seizures, hypokalaemia
Small, water-soluble, poorly protein-bound, low volume of distribution = dialysable. If a poisoned patient has organ failure, ask the mnemonic before you ask anything else.

4 · 🚫 Drug dosing & nephrotoxin avoidance in AKI

Every AKI patient is a pharmacological minefield. Two duties: stop what is harming the kidney, and re-dose what the kidney can no longer clear. KDIGO makes medication review a core part of AKI care.

Stop the nephrotoxins — the "sick day" and "STOP" thinking

ClassWhy it harms the AKI kidney
NSAIDsBlock prostaglandin-mediated afferent vasodilation → drop GFR in a hypoperfused kidney
ACE inhibitors / ARBsBlock angiotensin-II efferent constriction → drop the pressure the failing glomerulus depends on
DiureticsWorsen the volume depletion driving pre-renal AKI
Aminoglycosides, amphotericin, contrast, calcineurin inhibitorsDirectly tubulotoxic / vasoconstrictive
Metformin, SGLT2 inhibitorsNot directly nephrotoxic but accumulate/predispose to lactic acidosis or volume issues — hold in acute illness
💡 "DAMN" drugs to hold in AKI / on sick days

Diuretics · ACE inhibitors/ARBs · Metformin (and other Metabolised-renally agents) · NSAIDs. Suspend them during any acute intercurrent illness with dehydration, review daily, and — importantly — remember to restart the prognostically important ones (ACE-i/ARB in heart failure or proteinuric CKD) once the patient recovers, rather than leaving them stopped forever.

Re-dose the renally-cleared drugs

  • Reduce or extend doses of renally-cleared drugs: many antibiotics (aminoglycosides, vancomycin — dose by levels), low-molecular-weight heparin (accumulates — anti-Xa monitor or switch to unfractionated), gabapentinoids, opioids (especially morphine — its active metabolite accumulates causing prolonged sedation), DOACs.
  • Beware fluctuating function — in evolving AKI, yesterday's creatinine underestimates today's impairment; dose conservatively and monitor levels.
⚠️ Metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA)

A patient with vomiting and diarrhoea develops AKI while still taking metformin. Metformin accumulates, inhibits mitochondrial respiration, and drives a severe type-B lactic acidosis — a high-anion-gap acidosis (session 13) that dialysis both clears the drug and corrects. Always ask whether the metformin was held. This is why 'hold metformin during acute illness' is not bureaucratic caution — it prevents a life-threatening, dialysis-requiring acidosis.

5 · 🔄 The AKI-to-CKD transition — burying the 'fully reversible' myth

Here is the most important idea in this entire nephrology block, and the one most often missed. The old teaching — "acute tubular necrosis recovers, the creatinine comes back to baseline, job done" — is dangerously wrong. AKI and CKD are not separate diseases; they are two ends of one continuum, and each drives the other.

Maladaptive repair — why the kidney does not simply heal

After significant injury, the kidney attempts to regenerate — but the repair is often maladaptive: tubular cells arrest in a pro-fibrotic state, secreting cytokines that drive interstitial fibrosis, glomerulosclerosis, capillary rarefaction and nephron loss. Surviving nephrons hyperfilter to compensate, which accelerates their own demise. So even when the serum creatinine drifts back toward "normal", nephron mass has been permanently lost — masked by hyperfiltration in the survivors.

An episode of AKI is not an event the kidney simply recovers from — it is an inflection point that raises the lifetime risk of CKD, future AKI, and cardiovascular death, even when the creatinine 'normalises.'
🎯 The hard numbers behind the myth-busting

A single episode of AKI is associated with roughly a 2–3× increased risk of developing CKD and around an 8–10× increased risk of end-stage renal disease, plus higher long-term mortality — risk that scales with the severity, duration and recurrence of the AKI (KDIGO stage). "Creatinine back to baseline" at discharge does not equal "kidney back to baseline." Every AKI survivor carries forward risk.

Closing the loop — structured follow-up (KDIGO)

  • Recheck renal function after discharge — KDIGO recommends re-evaluating at ~3 months to establish whether function recovered, a new CKD baseline has emerged, or CKD has progressed.
  • Nephrology referral for: incomplete recovery, AKI stage 3 or needing dialysis, a step-down in eGFR baseline, significant proteinuria, unclear cause, or recurrent AKI. (KDIGO/NICE thresholds.)
  • Ongoing care: blood-pressure control, RAAS inhibition for proteinuric CKD (restarted appropriately after recovery), nephrotoxin avoidance, medication review, an AKI 'alert' on the record, patient education on sick-day rules, and cardiovascular risk management.
☠️ M&M — the survivor nobody followed up

A 62-year-old man survived a stage-3 AKI on the ICU after septic shock (echoes of session 1). His creatinine 'came back to normal' by discharge, his ACE inhibitor and metformin were both stopped during the illness, and — reassured that the AKI had 'fully reversed' — no one arranged renal follow-up or restarted his cardioprotective ACE inhibitor. There was no discharge letter flag, no 3-month bloods, no BP review. Eighteen months later he re-presented with advanced CKD (eGFR 22), uncontrolled hypertension and heavy proteinuria, now needing pre-dialysis planning. What was missed: his 'normalised' creatinine hid substantial permanent nephron loss from maladaptive repair; the AKI had raised his CKD and ESRD risk many-fold; and the failure to follow up, control BP, and restart RAAS blockade let a modifiable trajectory run unchecked. Lessons: AKI is never assumed 'fully reversible'; every survivor gets documented follow-up, a 3-month re-check, medication reconciliation with appropriate restart of prognostic drugs, and referral by KDIGO criteria. The loop must be closed on paper, not just in the notes.

6 · 🧵 Synthesis — the whole 16-session conference in one thread

Step back and see the arc. Everything we have covered is one story: an insult reaches the kidney, deranges the internal environment, and either resolves or scars — and our job is to read it fast, treat mechanism-first, and close the loop afterwards.

ThreadWhere it ran through the conference
The insultSepsis and shock (Day 1 opening), nephrotoxins and contrast, toxins and toxic alcohols (this session), obstruction, glomerular disease
The derangementAcid–base I & II (sessions 13–14), the metabolic emergencies (session 15), fluid and electrolyte storms, hyperkalaemia
Reading it fastThe five-step ABG method, the anion & osmolar gaps, delta-delta, urine chloride/anion gap, Cairo–Bishop
Mechanism-first treatmentFix the maintainer not just the generator (alkalosis); block the enzyme then remove the poison (toxic alcohols); protect the kidney before you shift electrolytes (TLS, DKA)
Closing the loopNephrotoxin stewardship, drug re-dosing, the AKI-to-CKD transition, structured follow-up and referral
💡 The single sentence to carry out of the whole conference

Read the internal environment in the same disciplined order every time, treat the mechanism rather than the number on the screen, protect the kidney from the toxins and the drugs, and never assume the kidney simply 'recovered' — follow it up. Simple enough to remember; impossible to forget.

7 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Toxic alcohols run osmolar-gap-first, anion-gap-later. A normal osmolar gap late, or a normal anion gap early, does not exclude poisoning. Treat on suspicion: fomepizole (block alcohol dehydrogenase) + haemodialysis + cofactors.
  2. Salicylate = respiratory alkalosis + high-gap metabolic acidosis. Keep the blood/urine alkaline (ion-trapping, replace K⁺), never let them become acidaemic, and dialyse for level >700 mg/L, neurology, oedema, renal failure or refractory acidosis.
  3. Dialysable toxins — Lithium, Metformin/lactate, Salicylate, toxic alcohols, Valproate, Theophylline (small, water-soluble, low protein binding, low volume of distribution).
  4. In AKI, hold the DAMN drugs (Diuretics, ACE-i/ARB, Metformin, NSAIDs), re-dose renally-cleared drugs (opioids, LMWH, vancomycin, DOACs), and remember MALA.
  5. AKI is NOT 'fully reversible.' Maladaptive repair drives fibrosis and permanent nephron loss; one AKI raises CKD risk ~2–3× and ESRD risk ~8–10×. A normalised creatinine hides lost nephrons.
  6. Close the loop: 3-month re-check, KDIGO-criteria nephrology referral, BP control, appropriate RAAS restart, nephrotoxin stewardship, and a documented AKI flag with sick-day education.
  7. The conference in one line: read the internal environment in the same order every time, treat the mechanism not the number, protect the kidney, and follow it up.

moderatorQs.q: A patient with a suspected ethylene glycol ingestion has a normal anion gap. Does that reassure you?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — the timing is everything. Early after ingestion the toxic acids (glycolic, oxalic) have not yet been produced, so the anion gap can be normal while the osmolar gap is high from the unmetabolised parent alcohol. If I check only the anion gap early, I will be falsely reassured. Conversely, late in the course the osmolar gap closes as the alcohol is metabolised, just as the anion gap opens and the patient is most acidotic and most damaged. So a single normal gap of either kind never excludes toxic-alcohol poisoning. With a compatible history I would start fomepizole to block alcohol dehydrogenase immediately, arrange haemodialysis, give cofactors (thiamine/pyridoxine for ethylene glycol), and track the evolving anion gap, calcium, and renal function rather than trusting one number.

moderatorQs.q: Why does letting a salicylate-poisoned patient become acidaemic make them dramatically worse?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because pH governs where the salicylate goes. Salicylic acid crosses cell membranes in its protonated (un-ionised) form; the ionised form is trapped in the compartment it is in. As the blood becomes more acidic, a greater fraction of salicylate is protonated and crosses into the central nervous system, worsening neurotoxicity, seizures and death. This is why the protective respiratory alkalosis matters, and why intubating and under-ventilating such a patient — abolishing their compensatory hyperventilation and letting the pH fall — can be catastrophic. Management runs the other way: keep the blood alkaline, alkalinise the urine with bicarbonate to ion-trap salicylate in the tubule and enhance excretion (replacing potassium so the urine will alkalinise), and dialyse severe cases. Protect the pH and you keep the drug out of the brain.

moderatorQs.q: A patient's creatinine returned to baseline after a stage-3 AKI. What follow-up do they still need and why?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: They need structured follow-up regardless of the 'normal' creatinine, because a normalised creatinine masks permanent nephron loss from maladaptive repair — a single AKI raises the risk of CKD roughly 2–3-fold and of ESRD around 8–10-fold, scaled to its severity. KDIGO advises re-evaluating renal function at about 3 months to define the new baseline and detect progression, with nephrology referral for incomplete recovery, stage-3/dialysis-requiring AKI, a dropped eGFR baseline, significant proteinuria, unclear cause or recurrence. Alongside that: blood-pressure control, appropriate restart of RAAS inhibition that was held during the illness, nephrotoxin stewardship, medication reconciliation, an AKI flag on the record, and sick-day education. The 'AKI fully reversed' label without any of this is exactly how a modifiable trajectory to CKD gets missed.

audienceQs.q: I've got a metabolic acidosis with a high osmolar gap but I can't get toxic-alcohol levels for hours. Do I have to wait?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — treat empirically now. If the story fits (suspected methanol or ethylene glycol ingestion) and there is a high anion-gap acidosis and/or a raised osmolar gap, start fomepizole immediately to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase and stop further production of the toxic acid metabolites — every hour of delay is more formate hitting the optic nerve or oxalate hitting the tubules. Give cofactors (folinic acid for methanol; thiamine and pyridoxine for ethylene glycol), correct acidaemia, and call nephrology/ICU for haemodialysis, which removes both the parent alcohol and the toxic acids and corrects the acidosis. Waiting for a confirmatory level before treating is the classic error — the antidote is safe and the window to prevent blindness or dialysis-dependent AKI is short.

audienceQs.q: Which drugs on the chart should I be halting the moment an inpatient develops an AKI?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Think DAMN first: Diuretics (worsen pre-renal depletion), ACE inhibitors/ARBs (drop the efferent tone the failing glomerulus relies on), Metformin (accumulates → lactic acidosis, MALA) and other renally-cleared agents, and NSAIDs (block protective afferent vasodilation). Also hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness, and flag directly nephrotoxic agents — aminoglycosides, amphotericin, calcineurin inhibitors, and iodinated contrast. Then dose-adjust the renally-cleared drugs the patient must stay on: reduce/monitor vancomycin and aminoglycosides by levels, switch or monitor LMWH (anti-Xa), reduce gabapentinoids and DOACs, and watch morphine (its active metabolite accumulates → prolonged sedation). And put a note to restart the ACE inhibitor/ARB once function recovers, so a prognostically important drug isn't stopped forever.

audienceQs.q: How do I actually remember which poisonings are worth dialysing?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Use the property test and a short list. A toxin is dialysable if it is small, water-soluble, minimally protein-bound, and has a small volume of distribution — i.e. it stays in the blood where the dialyser can grab it. The six to keep on-call are Lithium, Metformin (with lactic acidosis), Salicylate, toxic alcohols (methanol/ethylene glycol), Valproate and Theophylline — remember the classic ISTUMBLE mnemonic (Isopropanol, Salicylates, Theophylline, Uraemia, Methanol, Barbiturates, Lithium, Ethylene glycol) and add metformin and valproate. The trigger to actually call renal is the same as any: a poisoned patient with organ failure, severe refractory acidosis, a dangerously high level, or clinical deterioration despite supportive care. When those line up with a toxin on that list, dialysis is both clearing the poison and often correcting the acidosis at the same time.
